clips.text_zh: BTC XRP DOGE 又係炒 maid 跟單就贏，我自己就係反指標每次都接刀 🧐 又係學費入埋今個月個倉。命理都話我今個月破財，我認命 ok。
clips.text_en_b1: BTC. XRP. DOGE. All you literally had to do was follow the maid. That is all you had to hold. Anons on /biz/ are pointing out that anyone who simply held these three coins through the recent cycle would be up right now, while most traders tried to time the moves and got chopped up.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread mocking traders who didn't just hold BTC/XRP/DOGE

signal.rationale: OP implies holding BTC/XRP/DOGE was the right play all along, weakly bullish

clips.text_en_b2: BTC, XRP, DOGE — anyone who simply held through the cycle would be sitting on gains right now. Anons on /biz/ are pointing out that traders who tried to time the market ended up chopped up, while straightforward buy-and-hold turned out to be the winning strategy. Despite this obvious pattern, plenty of people keep picking up the knife and bleeding out on every dip. The only reliable play, it seems, was the one that required the least effort.
clips.text_en_c1: Anons on /biz/ have been hammering home a rather uncomfortable point: anyone who simply held BTC, XRP, and DOGE through the recent cycle would currently be sitting on gains, whereas the majority of active traders who attempted to time entries and exits got chopped to pieces. The so-called 'maid signal,' in other words, would have outperformed virtually every discretionary strategy. That said, yours truly remains what the board affectionately calls a reverse indicator, having caught every falling knife this cycle and contributed yet another tuition payment to the market. If fortune-telling is to be believed, this month is supposedly one of financial hemorrhage.
clips.text_en_c2: The irony could scarcely be more pronounced: BTC, XRP, and DOGE constituted precisely the trio that any prudent observer ought to have simply held throughout this most recent cycle, rather than attempting the futile exercise of market-timing. A consensus has crystallised among /biz/ commentators that passive conviction in these three assets would have yielded returns that active traders — perpetually chopping themselves into pieces through ill-judged entries and exits — conspicuously failed to capture. The original poster, with characteristic self-deprecation, positions himself as the inverse indicator, absorbing losses at precisely the wrong junctures and surrendering yet another month to the tuition fees of financial naivety.

clips.text_zh: DOGE 又有人儲到 25k 想買 AE86 😅 我就連蝕緊都未停，prop firm 個 account 又爆咗一個。搞掂100K先算啦。
clips.text_en_b1: I have 9,150 DOGE. Should I try to build up to 25,000 in case it does hit one pound? I want to buy a Toyota AE86. The anon is asking whether to keep DCA-ing DOGE to reach 25k coins as a moonshot bet on a JDM car.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ anon asking about accumulating DOGE to 25k for an AE86

signal.rationale: Anon's accumulation goal of 25k DOGE to buy an AE86 is an implicit long bet

clips.text_en_b2: An anon has been stacking DOGE and is now sitting on roughly 9,150 coins, hoping to push that figure up to 25,000 in case the token actually hits one pound. The end goal is laughably specific: he wants to buy a Toyota AE86, the JDM cult classic. Meanwhile, my own prop firm account just got blown again, so I am stuck bleeding red while day traders chase moonshot bets on glorified meme coins. Hitting 100K first, then maybe dreaming.
clips.text_en_c1: A fellow /biz/ anon has reached the 25,000 DOGE threshold and is now contemplating whether to convert that position into a Toyota AE86, the quintessential JDM grail. His rationale, as best I can reconstruct it, is that should DOGE ever breach the symbolic one-pound mark, the proceeds would be sufficient to acquire the vehicle outright. The question he has posed to the thread is whether continued dollar-cost averaging remains prudent given the speculative nature of the target. Meanwhile, your correspondent cannot even afford to pause the bleeding; another prop firm account went up in smoke this week, and the path to a hundred-K seems increasingly remote.
clips.text_en_c2: The proposition before the thread is deceptively whimsical in its specificity: should one methodically accumulate Dogecoin until the holdings reach the psychologically significant threshold of 25,000 coins, in the optimistic scenario that the asset appreciates to one pound sterling, thereby enabling the acquisition of a Toyota AE86 — that iconic Japanese domestic market machine beloved of petrolheads and Initial D devotees alike? The original poster, currently in possession of 9,150 DOGE and actively bleeding capital, finds himself unable to cease dollar-cost-averaging into a position that continues to underperform, even as yet another proprietary trading firm account detonates beneath the weight of his leveraged conviction. The interim objective is modest: reach one hundred thousand before entertaining any automotive fantasies whatsoever.

clips.text_zh: AI 寫 code 嘅帖又嚟，講真我而家 HKIE 溫書都靠 AI 續命 🙏 但 review 同改錯嘅時間都唔少，廢柴如我只係想快啲過牌。
clips.text_en_b1: Are there any recent studies that analyze whether AI helps productivity for SWE or SRE? Current LLMs either one-shot the task, which saves time but costs tokens, or they mess it up in many subtle ways that would never pass code review. For research tasks they leave you misinformed unless you re-verify everything yourself.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread asking about real studies on AI coding productivity

signal.rationale: No trade setup, just an AI productivity observation

clips.text_en_b2: Are there any recent studies that actually measure whether LLMs genuinely boost productivity for SWEs and SREs? From what I have seen, current models either one-shot the whole task, which saves time but burns through tokens at an alarming rate, or they produce output riddled with subtle errors that would never survive code review. On top of that, for research work they essentially leave you misinformed unless you painstakingly verify everything yourself.
clips.text_en_c1: A perennial thread on /g/ has resurfaced, canvassing opinions on whether contemporary LLMs genuinely enhance productivity for software and site reliability engineers, or whether the apparent gains are offset by hidden costs. The consensus, insofar as one exists, suggests a bifurcated outcome: when the model succeeds, it delivers a working solution in a single pass, thereby saving considerable effort at the expense of token consumption; when it fails, the errors are sufficiently subtle that they would never survive a competent code review. For research-oriented tasks, the situation is arguably worse, as users risk being subtly misinformed unless they independently re-verify every claim.
clips.text_en_c2: A perennial inquiry resurfaces on /g/ concerning empirical research into whether contemporary large language models genuinely augment the productivity of software and site reliability engineers, or merely furnish the illusion of accelerated output whilst imposing hidden costs. The consensus, insofar as one can be discerned, is bifurcated: when these models succeed, they produce functional code in a single pass, sparing considerable effort yet expending tokens with profligate abandon; when they fail, however, they introduce subtle, insidious defects that no competent reviewer would countenance. For research-oriented tasks, they leave the user not merely uninformed but actively misinformed, unless every claim is painstakingly re-verified against authoritative sources. The original poster, candidly self-identifying as inadequate, nonetheless relies upon AI to sustain his HKIE examination preparation — a dependency he frames as survival rather than enhancement.

clips.text_zh: /pol/ 又出 IQ 帖講統計平均數，講真我喺美國讀 civil engineering 時低 IQ 同學真係唔少 lol。HK 連空氣都唔夠用，想返美國。
clips.text_en_b1: The quickest way to test someone's intelligence is to make a generalized statement about a group. Say something like 'Asian men are shorter on average.' If they reply with 'not all Asian men are short,' you are dealing with someone genuinely low IQ. They cannot understand abstract ideas like a statistical average or per capita.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ post claiming statistical generalization is an IQ filter

signal.rationale: No trade setup, just a culture/political observation

clips.text_en_b2: The quickest way to gauge someone's actual intelligence is to throw out a perfectly reasonable statistical observation about a demographic — for instance, that Asian men tend to be shorter on average. If they jump in with 'not all Asian men are short,' you are dealing with someone who fundamentally cannot grasp the concept of a statistical average. They lack the abstract reasoning needed to understand per capita figures or general trends versus individual cases.
clips.text_en_c1: A /pol/ poster has proffered what he considers an elegant heuristic for gauging cognitive ability: make a generalised statement regarding a demographic group, such as claiming that Asian men are, on average, of shorter stature, and observe the response. Anyone who objects with 'not all Asian men are short,' the argument runs, has failed to grasp the abstract concept of a statistical mean or per-capita distribution, thereby betraying a fundamental intellectual limitation. Having studied civil engineering in the United States, I can attest that the theory holds rather more water than one might expect. Hong Kong, by contrast, offers neither the professional opportunities nor, frankly, sufficient breathable air.
clips.text_en_c2: A proposition circulating on /pol/ suggests that the swiftest intelligence assessment lies not in any formal psychometric instrument but in the careful observation of how an interlocutor responds to a generalised statistical observation. The illustrative example offered is characteristically blunt: declare that Asian men are, on average, shorter than their counterparts of other demographics, and observe the response. Should the person reply with the rejoinder that not all Asian men are short, the conclusion is merciless — one is contending with an individual of genuinely limited cognitive capacity, incapable of grasping abstract notions such as statistical central tendency, per capita measurement, or the difference between aggregate tendencies and individual instances.

clips.text_zh: Game dev 預算 30M vs 2 BILLION 😂 我而家 Surveying assistant 月份糧都唔夠交租，命理又話唔適合轉工，再捱多排考完牌先算。
clips.text_en_b1: 2012 versus 2026. Thirty million dollar budget versus two billion dollar budget. One hundred and twenty developers versus six thousand developers. Anons are comparing modern AAA game production costs and headcount against a 2012 baseline, asking where all the money and people actually went.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread comparing 2012 vs 2026 AAA dev budgets

signal.rationale: No trade setup, just a gaming industry observation

clips.text_en_b2: Take 2012 and line it up against 2026: back then a flagship title ran on roughly thirty million dollars and a lean team of around 120 developers, whereas today production budgets have ballooned to an almost absurd two billion dollars with six thousand people attached. Anons on /v/ are asking the obvious question — where exactly did all that extra money and headcount actually go? Meanwhile I am scraping by as a surveying assistant, so forgive me for not crying for the industry.
clips.text_en_c1: Anons on /v/ have been juxtaposing 2012 and 2026 AAA production figures with rather unsettling results: a thirty-million-dollar budget against a two-billion-dollar one, and roughly one hundred and twenty developers against six thousand, the latter figure representing modern headcount alone. The implicit question, which the thread has been wrestling with at considerable length, is precisely where that sixty-seven-fold increase in expenditure and fifty-fold increase in personnel has actually been allocated, given that the output rarely appears to scale accordingly. As a surveying assistant whose monthly paycheque barely covers rent, such figures are frankly demoralising.
clips.text_en_c2: The juxtaposition is staggering enough to provoke incredulity: thirty million dollars in 2012, allocated across a development team of one hundred and twenty, set against two billion dollars in 2026, dispersed among six thousand developers — a headcount expansion of fifty-fold against a budget increase of nearly seventy-fold, with no corresponding improvement in creative output that anyone can readily identify. Anons on /v/ are dissecting this arithmetic with forensic intent, attempting to ascertain precisely where the surplus capital and personnel have been dissipated, whether through managerial bloat, marketing extravagance, or the sheer gravitational pull of feature creep.

clips.text_zh: /fit/ 佬減脂減到連心肺都爆，我同肥仔信都係咁 😅 想打 MMA 都唔夠力，weight cut 簡直係地獄。命理話下個月運勢OK，希望啦。
clips.text_en_b1: How the fuck are you able to lift heavy and get enough protein on this shit? I lost 45 pounds in 3 months but I definitely lost muscle and strength. Being at the gym kills me. My heart gets destroyed by a set of squats and I feel like I am going to die.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ anon struggling to lift heavy while cutting hard

signal.rationale: No trade setup, just a fitness/cutting observation

clips.text_en_b2: How on earth are you supposed to keep lifting heavy and hitting your protein targets while cutting this hard? I dropped about 45 pounds in roughly three months, and although the number on the scale looked promising, I definitely sacrificed a fair amount of muscle and strength along the way. A single set of squats now leaves my heart rate absolutely wrecked, and forcing myself to eat more than twice a day feels like punishment.
clips.text_en_c1: A /fit/ regular has documented a rather harrowing cutting phase: forty-five pounds shed in three months, accompanied by what he describes as a catastrophic erosion of both muscular strength and cardiovascular capacity. The account is unflinching in its detail; a single working set of squats leaves him convinced that imminent cardiac arrest is a genuine possibility, and the caloric deficit has reduced him to perhaps two meals daily. His aspiration of competing in MMA now feels increasingly remote, as the requisite power output simply cannot be maintained under such conditions. Fortune-telling, mercifully, suggests that next month's prospects may improve.
clips.text_en_c2: The /fit/ lament articulates a physiological predicament familiar to anyone who has attempted aggressive caloric deficit whilst simultaneously preserving any pretence of athletic capacity: the poster has shed forty-five pounds across a mere three-month interval, a feat achieved at considerable cost to both muscular mass and strength reserves, such that even rudimentary compound movements now induce cardiovascular distress that borders on the syncopal. Squats, formerly a manageable staple, have become a form of self-punishment; the heart protests each set with alarming vehemence, whilst appetite suppression renders adequate protein intake a logistical impossibility. The aspiration toward mixed martial arts competition grows correspondingly remote, since weight cuts undertaken from such an enervated baseline are nothing short of purgatorial.

clips.text_zh: 又講神結局，我 Gundam 00 同 Attack on Titan 都係好睇 😅 Demon Slayer 第二季就麻麻。希望我人生都唔好爛尾啦，搞掂100K返美國先。
clips.text_en_b1: Years later and this is probably still the best anime ending I have ever seen. Why are there barely any other anime that tie up all of their plot points and loose ends in such a satisfying way? Is it an industry or writing problem? Anon is asking why satisfying anime endings feel so rare now.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread about the best anime ending ever made

signal.rationale: No trade setup, just an anime culture observation

clips.text_en_b2: Years on and I would still argue this is probably the best anime ending I have ever come across. The real puzzle is why so few modern series manage to wrap up their plot threads and resolve lingering loose ends in such a satisfying manner. Is it fundamentally a writing problem, or does it simply reflect broader industry rot? Personally I will take a Gundam 00 or Attack on Titan finale over most of what gets produced today.
clips.text_en_c1: Years after the fact, an /a/ regular maintains that a particular series still constitutes the finest conclusion he has encountered in the medium, and he has posed a question that the thread has been unable to resolve: why do so few anime manage to tie up their narrative threads and thematic strands in a comparably satisfying manner? The diagnosis remains contested; some attribute the trend to industry-wide structural pressures, while others place the blame squarely on declining writing standards. Personal favourites such as Gundam 00 and Attack on Titan illustrate that the capacity exists, whereas Demon Slayer's second season arguably demonstrates the opposite.
clips.text_en_c2: Years have elapsed since the broadcast in question, yet the conviction persists, undiminished by subsequent viewings or by the passage of intervening seasons, that the denouement in question remains the apogee of narrative resolution within the anime medium. The complaint is neither novel nor idiosyncratic: why, the poster inquires with weary frustration, do so few contemporary series bring their constituent plot threads and unresolved tensions to conclusions that feel genuinely cathartic rather than perfunctory or openly cynical? Gundam 00 and Attack on Titan receive honourable mention as exemplars of the form, whilst Demon Slayer's second season is dispatched with curt disparagement. Whether the deficiency lies in industrial economics, in creative exhaustion, or in the demands of an audience conditioned to perpetual sequelisation remains a matter for conjecture.
